nameStory: The Fingered Cobweaver gets its name from the distinctive finger-like projections on the male's reproductive structures, which spider experts use to identify the species. Like other cobweavers, it spins the classic messy, three-dimensional webs we often call cobwebs - those tangled masses of silk that catch dust in forgotten corners.
description: The Fingered Cobweaver is a small, round-bodied spider that belongs to the comb-footed spider family. These spiders have globular abdomens and relatively thin legs, giving them a somewhat delicate appearance. They're quite small, typically measuring just a few millimeters across. As cobweavers, they create irregular, sticky webs rather than the neat orb webs many people picture when thinking of spider webs.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Round, balloon-like abdomen that feels soft and appears almost translucent in good light, with a much smaller, harder-looking front section (cephalothorax)

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Irregular, three-dimensional tangle of silk threads that feels sticky to the touch - the classic 'cobweb' that lacks any organized pattern

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, with the body typically smaller than a pencil eraser, making them easy to overlook in their webs

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Thin, delicate-looking legs that appear almost thread-like, often held in a characteristic spread pattern while hanging in the web

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Hangs upside-down in its web, vibrating rapidly when disturbed, and often drops on a silk line when threatened

habitat: Found in sheltered areas throughout New England, particularly in wooded environments where they can build their webs between branches, under bark, or in natural crevices. They prefer spots protected from direct rain and wind, often in the understory of mixed hardwood and coniferous forests. Look for their webs in areas with some moisture but good air circulation.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build new webs in sheltered locations. This is when you're most likely to spot freshly constructed webs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible in their webs and mating occurs. Webs may be larger and more noticeable during this time.
seasonality.fall: Females may be carrying egg sacs or young spiders may be establishing their first webs. Activity begins to slow as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Most individuals overwinter in protected locations, often as juveniles or in egg sacs, with webs largely absent or abandoned.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that it's been documented only once in the entire region - making any sighting a truly special discovery that could contribute valuable information to our understanding of New England's spider diversity!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small comb-footed spiders, especially common house spiders, but the Fingered Cobweaver's more globular abdomen and specific web placement in natural (rather than human-made) structures can help distinguish it. When in doubt, the extreme rarity of this species means you're probably looking at a more common relative.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'cobweaver' comes from the old word 'coppe,' meaning spider, so cobweb literally means 'spider web.' Many people use 'cobweb' to refer specifically to old, dusty webs, but it actually describes the three-dimensional, irregular web structure that this entire family of spiders creates.
compareHints: Since this is the only Hentziectypus species in our region, compare it to other small comb-footed spiders like the common house spider or triangulate cobweaver. The Fingered Cobweaver tends to have a more perfectly round abdomen and prefers natural forest settings over the human-associated habitats favored by its more common relatives. Its web placement in wild areas rather than buildings is often the best clue.
